title: Energy Transformations

lessons.title: Recognize energy forms
lessons.question: How can the same energy appear in different forms?
ideas: Energy is the ability to do work or cause change. A moving bicycle has kinetic energy; a raised object or stored fuel has potential energy. Identify the object and the change before naming a form.
Sunlight, thermal energy, electrical energy and chemical energy can be inputs or outputs. Energy is transferred between objects and transformed between forms; it is not created during the change.
lessons.model: A cyclist eats food, pedals uphill, and coasts down. Chemical energy in food helps move the rider; some energy is stored as gravitational potential energy uphill and becomes kinetic energy downhill. Thermal energy also leaves the system.
lessons.check: Which object has gravitational potential energy?
options: A bicycle at the top of a hill
A stationary bicycle at the bottom of the hill
A bicycle bell after it stops ringing
lessons.writing: Trace two energy changes in a trip you know. Identify the starting store, the useful output, and one other output.

lessons.title: Trace conversions and waste energy
lessons.question: Where does the energy go when a converter is inefficient?
ideas: An energy conversion can be described as input energy → converter → output energies. The useful output depends on the job: motion is useful for a fan, while light is useful for a lamp.

Energy is conserved even when a device is inefficient. The difference between input energy and useful output often becomes thermal or sound energy dispersed to the surroundings. “Wasted” means not useful for the intended job.
lessons.model: For a hair dryer, electrical energy enters. Moving air and heat are intended outputs; sound is an additional output. If the goal is drying hair, both moving air and heat can be useful.
lessons.check: A lamp releases light and heat. What does “waste heat” mean?
options: Heat that is not useful for the lamp’s lighting job
lessons.writing: Draw or describe an input–converter–output chain for one home device. Explain which output is useful and why.

lessons.title: Generate electricity
lessons.question: How does motion at a generator become electrical energy?
ideas: A generator uses relative motion between a magnet and a coil of wire to produce electric energy. A turbine supplies the turning motion in many power stations.

Hydroelectric plants use moving water to turn turbines. Thermal plants heat water to make steam; nuclear fission can supply that heat. Compare the whole energy pathway and its environmental tradeoffs, not just the generator.
lessons.model: At a hydroelectric station, stored water → moving water → rotating turbine → generator → electrical energy. The generator changes the form of energy; the dam supplies the initial energy pathway.
lessons.check: What directly turns a generator in many power stations?
lessons.writing: Compare a hydroelectric and a thermal pathway. Name the different input and the shared conversion step.

lessons.title: Calculate power, energy and efficiency
lessons.question: Why do watts and kilowatt-hours answer different questions?
ideas: Power is the rate of energy transfer: power = energy ÷ time. A watt is one joule per second. Energy used over a period is power × time; electricity bills commonly use kilowatt-hours.

Efficiency compares useful output energy with input energy. Divide useful output by input and multiply by 100%. An efficiency below 100% does not break conservation; other outputs carry the remaining energy.
lessons.model: A 100 W lamp used for 4 h consumes 400 Wh = 0.4 kWh. If 20 J of a 100 J input becomes useful light, efficiency is 20%. Keep the time unit consistent with the energy unit.
lessons.check: A 200 W device runs for 2 h. How much energy does it use?
lessons.writing: Calculate the energy used by a 60 W light over 5 h in Wh and kWh. Show the conversion.

lessons.title: Follow energy through living things
lessons.question: How do plants and animals obtain usable energy?
ideas: Photosynthesis uses light energy to make energy-rich glucose from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll that captures light.

Cellular respiration transfers chemical energy from glucose to a usable form in cells, usually using oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide and water. Energy available to consumers decreases along a food chain because living things use energy and release heat.
lessons.model: Sunlight → grass → mouse → owl is an energy pathway. Grass is the producer. The mouse and owl are consumers. Energy is transferred, but each level has less available energy than the level before.
lessons.check: Which organism first captures light in a food chain?
lessons.writing: Explain how photosynthesis and cellular respiration connect in a plant-and-animal system.

lessons.title: Fuel the body and maintain balance
lessons.question: Why do energy needs vary from person to person?
ideas: Metabolism includes the chemical reactions that keep an organism alive. Homeostasis is the maintenance of relatively stable internal conditions despite changes outside the body.

Carbohydrates, fats and proteins have different roles. Carbohydrates are a common immediate fuel; fats store energy and help insulate; proteins support growth and repair. Age, activity and body conditions affect energy needs.
lessons.model: A person walking in cold weather uses energy for movement and for maintaining body temperature. The same person resting in a warm room has a different energy demand.
lessons.check: What describes maintaining a relatively stable internal body temperature?
lessons.writing: Use an everyday example to explain how metabolism helps maintain homeostasis.

lessons.title: Explain fossil fuels and extraction
lessons.question: Where did the stored energy in coal, oil and natural gas begin?
ideas: Coal, crude oil and natural gas formed from ancient biological material over very long periods. Their chemical energy ultimately came from past sunlight captured by living things.
Coal can be mined; oil and gas deposits are located and drilled. Crude oil is a mixture separated into useful fractions during refining. These fuels are non-renewable on a human timescale.
lessons.model: The energy path for a fuel-powered bus is ancient sunlight → organisms → fossil fuel → combustion → engine motion and heat. Extraction, refining and use each have separate impacts.
lessons.check: Why are fossil fuels called non-renewable?
options: They form far more slowly than people use them
They are all manufactured in a day
lessons.writing: Trace one fossil fuel from its formation to a useful product, including one extraction or refining step.

lessons.title: Evaluate fossil-fuel consequences
lessons.question: How can we compare a useful energy source with its costs?
ideas: Combustion of a fossil fuel releases stored chemical energy. Carbon-containing fuels commonly produce carbon dioxide during complete combustion, while other emissions depend on fuel composition and conditions.
Burning fossil fuels adds greenhouse gases and can contribute to air pollution and acid deposition. A fair comparison names a specific benefit, emission or impact, and the evidence used.
lessons.model: A claim that a plant produces electricity says something about useful output; it does not show that every emission is harmless. Compare the energy supplied with measured effects and possible controls.
lessons.check: Which claim is supported by an energy-output measurement alone?
options: How much useful energy was delivered
That every environmental effect was eliminated
lessons.writing: Write a short recommendation about one fossil-fuel use. Give one benefit, one risk, and one way to reduce the risk.

sourceType: Brightspace textbook and workbook; newly authored online explanations and formative checks

glossary.energy: The ability to do work or cause change.
glossary.kinetic energy: Energy an object has because it is moving.
glossary.potential energy: Stored energy associated with position or arrangement.
glossary.input energy: Energy entering a device or process.
glossary.converter: A device or process that changes an energy form.
glossary.output energy: Energy leaving a device or process.
glossary.conservation of energy: Energy is transferred or transformed, but the total is not created or destroyed.
glossary.generator: A device that produces electrical energy using motion between a magnet and a coil.
glossary.turbine: A rotating device driven by moving water, steam or another fluid.
glossary.hydroelectric: Electric generation that uses moving water as the energy source.
glossary.thermal generation: Electric generation in which heat helps produce turbine motion.
glossary.power: The rate at which energy is transferred or used.
glossary.watt: A unit of power equal to one joule per second.
glossary.kilowatt-hour: A unit of energy equal to using one kilowatt for one hour.
glossary.efficiency: Useful output energy divided by input energy, often stated as a percentage.
glossary.photosynthesis: A process in which plants use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
glossary.cellular respiration: A process that transfers energy from food molecules for cell use.
glossary.producer: An organism that makes its own energy-rich food, usually using light.
glossary.consumer: An organism that obtains energy by eating other organisms or their products.
glossary.metabolism: All chemical reactions that keep an organism functioning.
glossary.homeostasis: Maintenance of relatively stable internal conditions.
glossary.carbohydrate: A nutrient group that supplies energy and includes sugars and starches.
glossary.fat: A nutrient that stores energy and has structural and insulating roles.
glossary.protein: A nutrient used for growth, repair and many body functions.
glossary.fossil fuel: Fuel formed from ancient biological material over very long periods.
glossary.coal: A solid fossil fuel formed largely from ancient plant material.
glossary.crude oil: A liquid fossil-fuel mixture that can be refined into products.
glossary.natural gas: A gaseous fossil fuel consisting mainly of methane.
glossary.refining: Separating and processing crude oil into useful products.
glossary.combustion: A reaction with oxygen that releases energy, often as heat and light.
glossary.non-renewable: Used faster than it is naturally replaced on a human timescale.
glossary.greenhouse gas: A gas that absorbs and emits infrared radiation in Earth’s atmosphere.
glossary.acid deposition: Acidic substances deposited from the atmosphere in wet or dry form.
